name: Chest Pain
source_guidance: Adapted from NHS 111 and NHS public guidance on chest pain and heart attack symptoms, and WHO guidance on cardiovascular emergencies.

questions.text: Has the person collapsed, or are they unresponsive or not breathing normally?
Is there severe difficulty breathing, or are the lips blue or grey?
Has the chest pain lasted more than five minutes, or does it feel crushing or heavy?
Is the pain spreading to the arm, jaw, or back, or is the person sweaty or faint?
Does the person have known heart disease, and is this pain different from usual?
Is the pain worse on breathing in, or is there a cough with fever?
Is the pain only felt when pressing on the chest wall, or did it start after an injury?

emergency: Call 112 now, or get to the nearest hospital emergency department immediately.
Do not drive yourself. Ask someone to take you, or wait for the ambulance.
Sit the person down and keep them calm and still while waiting for help.
If the person becomes unresponsive and is not breathing normally, start chest compressions if trained.
Call back at once if symptoms get worse or new symptoms appear.
urgent: Go to a hospital or clinic today and be seen within the next few hours.
Take a list of current medicines with you.
Rest and avoid physical effort until seen.
If the pain becomes severe, crushing, or spreads to the arm or jaw, call 112 immediately.
routine: Book a clinic appointment within the next few days.
Rest the area and avoid heavy lifting.
Paracetamol can be taken as directed on the pack for pain.
Call back at once if symptoms get worse or new symptoms appear.
self_care: The answers do not point to a serious cause at this time.
Rest and avoid heavy effort today.
Paracetamol can be taken as directed on the pack.
Call back or call 112 at once if the pain becomes heavy or crushing, spreads, or comes with breathlessness, sweating, or fainting.
